headline: Junior ADU Construction: Preparing for Your Permit Application
articleBody:
Getting ready to build a Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit (JADU) is a smart move for adding value and flexibility to your home. While JADUs are generally simpler to permit than full ADUs, a smooth application process hinges on good preparation. Skipping steps here can lead to delays, so let's get you squared away to make sure your project in Long Beach or Cerritos goes as smoothly as possible.

First things first: you'll need to confirm that your property and the specific space you plan to convert actually qualify for a JADU. Remember, a JADU must be entirely contained within your existing single-family residence and can't exceed 500 square feet. Before you even think about designs, double-check these fundamental requirements against your property's actual layout. This foundational check ensures you're pursuing the right type of unit from the start, avoiding the frustration of redesigns if your space doesn't fit the JADU definition.

Next, take a good look at your existing structure. You'll need to verify the condition of the walls, windows, and any load-bearing elements. Think about the basics like egress (emergency exits), proper ventilation, and the capacity of your current utilities—especially electrical and plumbing. Does your electrical panel have enough juice for a small kitchen and a separate living space? Are the existing plumbing lines adequate? These are crucial details that will factor into your architectural plans and are often flagged during plan check if not properly addressed initially.

One of the defining features of a JADU is its efficiency kitchen and a separate entrance. Before submitting your permit application, you'll need a clear design for both. The efficiency kitchen doesn't need to be huge, but it must include cooking facilities and a sink. Think about the layout: where will the mini-fridge go, the stovetop, the counter space? For the separate entrance, consider its placement to ensure privacy for both the JADU occupant and the main household, and that it meets accessibility and safety codes. Having these design elements clearly laid out, even in preliminary sketches, will greatly aid the formal planning stage.

Finally, you'll need to prepare all the necessary documentation. This typically includes architectural plans detailing the layout, electrical, and plumbing changes, as well as a site plan showing the JADU's location within the primary residence and the separate entrance. You'll also need to fill out the specific permit application forms required by your local permitting agency. Don't forget that local jurisdictions often have their own specific forms or requirements beyond the state mandates, so check their website or give them a call to ensure you have everything needed for a 'complete application,' which is key for triggering that 60-day review period.

Questions to Ask Before You Decide

Before you finalize your plans, ask your chosen contractor or designer about their experience with JADU projects specifically, not just general remodels. Inquire about how they handle the coordination of architectural and structural plans, their familiarity with your local permitting agency, and their process for addressing plan-check comments. Understanding their approach to existing building conditions and ensuring they can provide code-compliant kitchen layouts are also crucial questions to ask. This will help you select a team that truly understands the nuances of JADU construction.
